label: P.HBetc
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P.HBetc}
	Suppose that $X$ is a separable Banach space (real or complex). Then the following results hold.
	
	 
	\begin{enumerate}
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
		\item \label{1.BS.HBe} Hahn--Banach extension theorem: For every subspace $Y$ of $X$ and a bounded linear functional $\varphi$ on $Y$, there is a linear functional $\psi$ on $X$ that extends $\varphi$ and has the same norm as $\varphi$. 
		                                             
		\item \label{2.BS.BA} Banach--Alaoglu theorem: The closed unit ball $\mathbf B(X^*)$ of the dual space $X^*$ is weak*-compact. 
		\item \label{3.BS.w*} The weak* topology on $\mathbf B(X^*)$ is compact, metrizable, and separable. 
		\item \label{4.BS.KM} Krein--Milman theorem: If $K$ is a weak*-compact and convex subset of $X^*$, then $K$ is the closed convex hull of its extreme boundary, $\partial K$. 
		\item \label{5.BS.HBs} Hahn--Banach separation theorem: If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint convex subsets of $X$ and $A$ is open, then there is $\varphi\in X^*$ such that $Re(\varphi(x))<\inf_{y\in B} Re(\varphi(y))$ for all $x\in A$.
		\item \label{6.BS.OM}  The Open Mapping Theorem, Closed Graph Theorem, and
		Uniform Boundedness Theorem hold for maps with domain $X$ (and separable codomain for the Closed Graph Theorem). 
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x_n$, for $n\in \mathbb{N}$, be an enumeration of a dense subset of the unit ball of $X$.

\eqref{1.BS.HBe} It suffices to prove this in the case when $X$ is a real Banach space. The standard proof, using Zorn's Lemma (e.g., \cite[Lemma 2.3.2]{pedersen2012analysis}), can be performed using a countable dense set instead, as follows.
 Then $Y_n=\operatorname{span}(Y\cup \{x_j\mid j\leq n\})$ defines an increasing sequence of linear subspaces of $X$ with dense union. Let $Y_0=Y$ and $\psi_0=\varphi$.  The standard proof of the Hahn--Banach theorem shows that for every $n$ and linear functional $\psi_n$ on $Y_n$ there is a closed interval $[\alpha,\beta]$ in $\mathbb R$ such that  for any $\gamma\in [\alpha,\beta]$,  $\psi_{n+1}(y+tx_n)=\psi_n(y)+t\gamma$   extends $\psi_n$  to $Y_{n+1}$ and satisfies $\|\psi_n\|=\|\psi_{n+1}\|$. Use $\gamma=\alpha$ to define $\psi_{n+1}$.  This defines $\psi$ on $\bigcup_nY_n$, and $\psi$ extends
 to $X$ by continuity. 
                                                                        
	
	
	
	\eqref{2.BS.BA}	For the Banach--Alaoglu theorem, note that the evaluation map from $\mathbf B(X^*)$ into $\mathbb{D}^n$ (where $\mathbb{D}$ denotes the closed unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$) defined by $\varphi\mapsto (\varphi(x_n))$ is, by the standard proof, a homeomorphism onto its range. Since~$\mathbb{D}$ is homeomorphic to $[0,1]^2$, and since $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ is compact by Tychonoff's theorem (no choice needed, cf.\ \cite[XII.11.6.9]{BlackadarReal}), $\mathbb{D}^\mathbb{N}$ is compact. The range of the evaluation map is closed, hence compact. 
	
	\eqref{3.BS.w*}	The standard metric on $\mathbf B(X^*)$, 
	\[
	d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_n 2^{-n}|\varphi(x_n)-\psi(x_n)|
	\]
	is as required, by the standard proof.  $\mathbf B(X^*)$ is second countable, hence separable by
	\cite[XII.15.9.8]{BlackadarReal}. 
	
	\eqref{4.BS.KM} and 	\eqref{5.BS.HBs}: While we don’t know ordinary proofs of these assertions that do not use the Axiom of Choice, we can 	prove that a proof exists. See  \ref{S.KreinMilman} and  \ref{S.HBseparation}.
		
	\eqref{6.BS.OM}:  The Baire Category Theorem for separable complete metric spaces
	requires no Choice.  The proofs of the Open Mapping Theorem and Uniform Boundedness 
	Theorem (second proof) as written in \cite{BlackadarReal} require no additional choice
	(in the proof in XVIII.8.2.5 the $x_n$ can be systematically chosen from a dense sequence),
	and the Closed Graph Theorem is a simple corollary of the Open Mapping Theorem.
head: environment

label: P.WO.HB
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P.WO.HB}
	Suppose that $X$ is a Banach space with a well-ordered dense subset. Then the Hahn--Banach extension theorem holds for $X$. \qed
head: environment

label: ClosedSubspaceProp
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: ExtensionProp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{ExtensionProp}
	Let $X$ be a Banach space and $Y$ a closed subspace of~$X$.  Then $X$ is separable if and only
	if $Y$ is separable and there is a countable subset $C$ of~$X$ whose image in $X/Y$ (with the
	quotient norm) is dense.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $X$ is separable, then $Y$ is separable (\ref{ClosedSubspaceProp}), and a countable dense set
	in $X$ works for $C$.  Conversely, let $C$ be such a subset of $X$, and $D$ a countable dense
	subset of $Y$.  Then $C+D$ is countable.  Let $\pi:X\to X/Y$ be the quotient map.  Let $x\in X$
	and $\epsilon>0$.  Then there is a $c\in C$ with $\|\pi(x)-\pi(c)\|_{X/Y}=\|\pi(x-c)\|_{X/Y}<\epsilon$.
	From the definition of the quotient norm and density of $D$ in $Y$, there is a $d\in D$ with
	$$\|(x-c)-d\|_X=\|x-(c+d)\|_X<\epsilon$$
	and thus $C+D$ is dense in $X$.
head: environment

label: L.states
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{L.states}  Every separable $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra, and more generally every $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra with a well-ordered dense subset,  has sufficiently many states.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a separable $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A$. We may assume that $A$ is unital. Fix $x\in A$. 
	We will prove that there is a state $\varphi$ on $A$ such that $\varphi(x^*x)=\|x\|^2$. In particular, 
if $A$ is a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra and $x\in A$, then $x^*x\in A_+$ (Proposition~\ref{PropII313}), and it follows from functional
calculus that $\|\lambda 1+x^*x\|=\lambda+\|x^*x\|$ for any $\lambda\geq0$.  Thus, if $S$ is
the two-dimensional subspace of $A$ spanned by 1 and $x^*x$, the linear functional $\phi$ on $S$
defined by $\phi(1)=1$ and $\phi(x^*x)=\|x^*x\|=\|x\|^2$ has norm~1.

The Hahn--Banach Theorem for separable Banach spaces does not require any Choice (Proposition~\ref{P.HBetc}); in fact $\phi$ has an algorithmically constructed extension to $A$ of norm 1 (once a countable dense sequence is fixed).  Since a linear functional $\psi$ on $A$ is a state if and only if it has norm 1 and $\psi(1)=1$ \cite[II.6.2.5]{BlackadarOperator}, we conclude that a separable $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra  has sufficiently many states.
head: environment

label: L.S(A)
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L.S(A)}
	Suppose that $A$ is a separable unital  $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra. Then the state space $\mathsf S(A)$ with respect to the weak*-topology is a separable compact metrizable space. 
	The pure state space $\mathsf P(A)$ is a Borel (more precisely, $G_\delta$, i.e., $\Pi^0_2$ in modern descriptive-set theoretic notation, see \cite{Ke:Classical} or \cite[XV.3.4.1]{BlackadarReal}) subset of $\mathsf S(A)$. 
	
	If $A$ is commutative, unital,  and separable, then $X=\mathsf P(A)$ is a  compact metric space and $A\cong C(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The state space is nonempty by Lemma~\ref{L.states}. The standard proof that $\mathsf S(A)$ is a weak*-closed subset of the unit ball of the Banach space dual of $A$ requires no choice. By the Banach--Alaoglu theorem (Proposition~\ref{P.HBetc} \eqref{2.BS.BA}  and \eqref{3.BS.w*}), the latter is a separable compact metric space. 
	
	Finally, by the Krein--Milman theorem  for separable compact convex sets (a proof is provided in \ref{S.KreinMilman}), $\mathsf S(A)$  is the closed convex hull of the space of its extreme points, which is the space of pure states. 
	
	That $\mathsf P(A)$ is a $G_\delta$ is a standard result, see.\ e.g.\  \cite[XVIII.9.5.10]{BlackadarReal}.
	
	The proof in case when $A$ is not necessarily separable but has a well-ordered dense subset is analogous and uses Proposition~\ref{P.WO.HB} (although $\mathsf P(A)$ will not be Borel in general).  
	
	Finally, if $A$ is unital and commutative then the standard proof that the space of characters is closed in $\mathsf S(A)$ and that it coincides with $\mathsf P(A)$ applies.
head: environment

label: FaithfulStateThm
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{FaithfulStateThm}
A separable $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra has a faithful state.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We may assume $A$ is unital.  Then $\mathsf S(A)$ is weak-* separable (\ref{L.S(A)}).
Let $(\phi_n)$ be a dense sequence in $\mathsf S(A)$, and set $\phi=\sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n}\phi_n$.  Then $\phi$ is a state on $A$.  We claim that~$\phi$ is faithful.  Fix a positive $a\in A$ of norm 1.
Then there is an (algorithmically constructed) state $\psi$ on $A$ with $\psi(a)=1$.
Approximating $\psi$ by a $\phi_n$, there is an $n$ with $\phi_n(a)>1/2$, and we have
$\phi(a)\geq2^{-n}\phi_n(a)>2^{-n-1}>0$.
head: environment

label: SpectrumThm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{SpectrumThm}
	Let $A$ be a unital  complex Banach algebra, and $x\in A$.
	Then $\sigma(x)$ is nonempty and compact, and
	\[
	\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\sigma(x)\}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|x^n\|^{1/n}=\inf_n\|x^n\|^{1/n}\ .
	\]
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $A$ be a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra, $x=x^*\in A$.  Then $\sigma(x)\subseteq[-\|x\|,\|x\|]$, and at least
	one of $\|x\|,-\|x\|$ is in $\sigma(x)$.  More generally, if $x$ is normal, then 
	$\|x\|=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\sigma(x)\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the $\mathrm{C}^*$-axiom, $\|x^{2^k}\|^{2^{-k}}=\|x\|$ for any $k$. 
	So we have that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \|x^n\|^{1/n}$ exists and equals $\inf_n\|x^n\|^{1/n}$,  and submultiplicativity of the norm implies $\|x^n\|^{1/n} \leq \|x\|$ for all $n$, so  we have $\|x^n\|^{1/n}=\|x\|$ for all~$n$.
	Thus the sequence in the statement of Theorem~\ref{SpectrumThm} is constant.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $A$ be a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra, $x$ a normal element of~$A$, and $p$ a polynomial with
	complex coefficients.  Then 
	\[
	\|p(x)\|=\max\{|p(\lambda)|:\lambda\in\sigma(x)\}.
	\]
head: environment

label: SAFunctCalc
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{SAFunctCalc}
	Let $A$ be a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra, and $x=x^*\in A$.  Then $p\mapsto p(x)$ ($p$ a complex polynomial)
	extends to an isometric
	isomorphism from $C(\sigma(x))$ onto $C^*(x,1)$, the uniformly closed subalgebra of $A$
	generated by $x$ and 1.
head: environment

label: PropII312
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{PropII312}
	Let $A$ be a (unital) $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra and $x\in A$.  Then
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(i)]  If $x\geq0$ and $-x\geq0$, then $x=0$.
		\item[(ii)]  If $x=x^*$, then $x^2\geq0$.
		\item[(iii)]  If $x\geq0$, then $\|x\|=\max\{\lambda:\lambda\in\sigma(x)\}$.
		\item[(iv)]  If $x=x^*$ and $\|x\|\leq2$, then $x\geq0$ if and only if $\|1-x\|\leq1$.
		\item[(v)]  If $x=x^*$ and $f\in C(\sigma(x))$, then $f(x)\geq0$ if and only if $f(t)\geq0$
		for all $t\in\sigma(x)$.
		\item[(vi)]  If $x=x^*$ there is a unique decomposition $x=x_+-x_-$ in $C^*(x)\subseteq A$
		with $x_+,x_-\in A_+$ and $x_+x_-=0$.  We have $x_+=f(x)$ and $x_-=g(x)$, where
		$f(t)=\max(t,0)$ and $g(t)=-\min(t,0)$.  Thus every element of $A$ is a linear combination
		of four elements of $A_+$.
		\item[(vii)]  Every positive element $x$ of $A$ has a unique (in $C^*(x)$) positive square root
		$x^{1/2}=f_{1/2}(x)$, where $f_{1/2}(t)=t^{1/2}$.  More generally, if $x\geq0$ and $\alpha$
		is a positive real number, there is a positive $x^\alpha=f_\alpha(x)\in C^*(x)_+$, where
		$f_\alpha(t)=t^\alpha$; these elements satisfy $x^\alpha x^\beta=x^{\alpha+\beta}$, 
		$(x^{\alpha})^\beta=x^{\alpha\beta}$, $x^1=x$,
		and $\alpha\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous.  If $x$ is invertible, $x^\alpha$ is also
		defined for $\alpha\leq0$, with the same properties.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: PropII313
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: UniquePosSqrtProp
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
There is a canonical $a=x^{1/2}\in C^*(x)\subseteq A$ with $a^2=x$ (Proposition~\ref{PropII312} (vii)).  It remains to prove uniqueness of the square root in $A$. 
	Since $a$ is a uniform
	limit of polynomials in $x$, it commutes with any element of $A$ which commutes with $x$.
	If $b$ is any positive element of $A$ with $b^2=x$, then $b$ commutes with $x$ and hence
	with $a$.  Thus, replacing $A$ with $C^*(a,b)$, we may assume $A$ is commutative.  Since
	$$0=a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)$$
	we have $a-b\perp a+b$, and thus $a-b\perp(a+b)^{1/2^n}$ for any $n\in\mathbb{N}$.  But $a$ and $b$, hence $a-b$,
	are in the hereditary $\mathrm{C}^*$-subalgebra of $A$ generated by $a+b$ (which is positive), and $\{(a+b)^{1/2^n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is an
	approximate unit for this hereditary $\mathrm{C}^*$-subalgebra, so we have
	$$0=(a-b)(a+b)^{1/2^n}\to a-b$$
	and hence $a-b=0$.
head: environment

label: T.SpectralMapping
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T.SpectralMapping} Suppose that $n\geq 1$ and $a_1,\dots, a_n$ are commuting normal elements of a $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A$. 
	Then $\operatorname{j\sigma}(a_1,\dots, a_n)$ is nonempty.
	If $f$ is a complex *-polynomial in $2n$ variables, then 
	\begin{multline*}
	\sigma(f(a_1,\dots, a_n, a_1^*,\dots, a_n^*))\\
	=\{f(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, \bar\lambda_1, \dots, \bar\lambda_n)\mid (\lambda_1,\dots, \lambda_n)\in \operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)\}. 
	\end{multline*}
head: environment

label: RepCAlg
title: Definition
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
A $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A$ is representable if and only if $A$ has enough states to determine its norm, i.e.
	$$\|x\|^2=\sup\{\phi(x^*x):\phi\in\mathsf S(A)\}$$
	for every $x\in A$, where $\mathsf S(A)$ is the set of states on $A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $A$ is representable, then vector states determine the norm.  Conversely, if states determine the norm,
	a direct sum of GNS representations is faithful (isometric).
head: environment

label: RepThm
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Proposition~\ref{P.Representable} it suffices to prove that $A$ has sufficiently many states, and this was shown in Lemma~\ref{L.states}.
head: environment

label: SepRepThm
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
If $A$ is a separable and  commutative $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra, then the Gelfand transform 
	\[
	A\ni a\mapsto \hat a\in C_0(\mathsf P(A))
	\]
	is an isomorphism. In particular, every separable commutative $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra is isomorphic to $C_0(X)$ for some locally compact metrizable space $X$.  If  $A$ is unital, then it is isomorphic to $C(X)$ for some compact metrizable space~$X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the assertion with the additional assumption that~$A$ is unital. By Lemma~\ref{L.states}, $A$ has sufficiently many states. Since the state space of $A$ is compact and metrizable,  the Krein--Milman theorem (\ref{S.KreinMilman}) implies that it is equal to the closed convex hull of the space of pure states of~$A$. Therefore the Gelfand transformation is isometric. The image of $A$ is a *-subalgebra of $C(\mathsf P(A))$ that contains all scalars and (by definition) separates the points. Since the Stone--Weierstrass theorem can be proved without the Axiom of Choice (\ref{S.CFC}), the map is an isomorphism as required. 
	
	If $A$ is not unital, consider its unitization $\tilde A$. Then $\mathsf P(A)$ is naturally identified with an open dense subspace of $\mathsf P(\tilde A)$ that separates the points in the image of $A$ under the Gelfand map, and $A$ is identified with $C_0(\mathsf P(A))$. The result follows from the already proved result for the unitization of $A$.
head: environment

label: P.Russell.example
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\eqref{1.Russell.example} Let $X=\bigsqcup_n X_n$ be a Russell set, where each $X_n$ is a two-element set.  We first define a universal $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A_0$ given by generators and relations; the existence of such algebra does not require any Choice.  We will then define a state~$\tau$ on $A_0$, and the required algebra will be the image of $A_0$ under the GNS representation associated with  $\tau$. 
	
	Generators of $A_0$ are $p_x$, for $x\in X$. The relations require that each $p_x$ is a projection (that is, $p_x=p_x^*=p_x^2$), that for every $n$ we have $\sum_{x\in X_n} p_x=1$, and that $[p_x,p_y]=0$ for all $x$ and $y$. 
	Thus $p_x p_y=0$ if and only if $x$ and $y$ are distinct and belong to the same $X_n$. The space of linear combinations of products $\prod_{x\in F} p_x$, where $F\subset X$ intersects each $X_n$ in at most one point (every such transversal is finite because $X$ is a Russell set), is a dense *-subalgebra of $A_0$. 
	On such  monomials define a functional by $\tau(\prod_{x\in F} p_x)=2^{-|F|}$. 
	We claim that $\|\tau\|=\tau(1)=1$. To see this, note that $\tau(1)=1$ and therefore $\|\tau\|\geq 1$.  To see that $\|\tau\|\leq 1$, take a finite linear combination $a$ of monomials in projections $p_x$. For a large enough $n$, $a$ is of the form $a=\sum_{x\in \prod_{j\leq n} X_j} \lambda_x \prod_{j\leq n} p_{x(j)}$ with complex coefficients $\lambda_{x}$. Then 
	\[
	|\tau(a)|=\biggl|2^{-n}\sum_{x\in \prod_{j\leq n} X_j} \lambda _x\biggr|\leq \max_{x\in \prod_{j\leq n} X_j} |\lambda_x|=\|a\|,
	\] 
	and $\|\tau\|\leq 1$ follows. It follows that $\tau$ is a contraction on a dense subalgebra of $A_0$. Its continuous extension to $A_0$ (denoted $\tau$ for convenience) still satisfies $\|\tau\|=\tau(1)=1$, and is therefore a state. Since $A_0$ is commutative, it is tracial. 
	
	
	Then $A=\pi_\tau[A_0]$ is a concrete commutative $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra. Fix $x\in X$. 
Since $\tau(p_x)=1/2$, $\pi_\tau(p_x)$ is a nonzero projection. 
In the following, for the simplicity of notation we  will write $p_x$ for $\pi_\tau(p_x)$.
	
	We need to prove that the pure state space of $A$ is empty. Assume $\varphi$ is a pure state on $A$. Then for every $n$ we would have $\varphi(p_x)=1$ for some $x\in X_n$, otherwise $\varphi$ would be a convex combination of $\psi_x(a)=\varphi (p_x a)/\varphi(p_x)$ and $\psi_y(a)=\varphi (p_y a)/\varphi(p_y)$, where $X_n=\{x,y\}$. 
	Thus from $\varphi$ one could define a subset of $X$, $\{x\in X\mid \varphi(p_x)=1\}$ that intersects each $X_n$ in exactly one point; contradiction. 
	
	This implies that the Gelfand spectrum of $A$ is empty, and therefore $A$ is not isomorphic to $C(Z)$ for a compact Hausdorff space $Z$. 
	
For each $n\geq 1$, let $Y_n=\bigsqcup_{1\leq k\leq n}X_k$.  Then $Y_n$ is a finite set with $2n$
elements, and $X$ is the increasing union of the $Y_n$. 
Let $A_n$ be the $\pi_\tau$-image of  set of linear combinations of projections of the form $\prod_{x\in F} p_x$, where $F\subset Y_n$ intersects each $X_k$ in at most one point.  Then $A_n$ is a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-subalgebra of $A$
isomorphic to ${\mathbb C}^{2^n}$,
$A_n\subseteq A_{n+1}$, and $\bigcup_nA_n$ is dense in $A$.  In fact, if $B_n$ is the $\mathrm{C}^*$-subalgebra
generated by $\{p_x:x\in X\setminus Y_n\}$, then $A$ is naturally isomorphic to 
$A_n\otimes B_n$.	


\eqref{2.Russell.example} Let $\mathsf S(A)$ be the state space of  the $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A$ as in \eqref{1.Russell.example}. $\mathsf S(A)$ can be described as an inverse limit of finite-dimensional
simplexes: there is an inverse
system
$$
\mathsf S(A)\to \cdots \to \mathsf S(A_{-n-1})\to \mathsf S(A_{-n})\to\cdots\to \mathsf S(A_{-2})\to \mathsf S(A_{-1})
$$
where the connecting maps are given by restriction.  $\mathsf S(A_n)$ is a $(2^n-1)$-simplex, and
the connecting maps send extreme points to extreme points.  The space $\mathsf S(A)$ can be
naturally put at the index $-\infty$, and the restriction maps from $\mathsf S(A)$ to $\mathsf S(A_n)$ separate points.  They are even surjective. This is because for every $\psi\in \mathsf S(A_n)$, the tensor product of $\psi$ and the restriction of $\tau$ to $B_n$ belongs to $\mathsf S(A)$.  

To see that $\mathsf S(A)$ is not compact (in the weak-* topology), let $K_n$ be the set of states of $A$ whose restriction to $A_n$
is a pure state. Then $K_n$ is closed since the pure state space of $A_n$ is closed, and
nonempty since the restriction map from $\mathsf S(A)$ to $\mathsf S(A_n)$ is surjective.  
So $(K_n)$ is a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets of $\mathsf S(A)$, and any element of $\bigcap_n K_n$ would define a choice function for $X$. Therefore $\bigcap_nK_n=\emptyset$
and $\mathsf S(A)$ is not compact.

title: Theorem
head: environment

label: OrthProjSeqProp
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(P_n)$ be a sequence of mutually orthogonal nonzero projections in ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal H})$, and let
		${\mathcal H}_n$ be the range of $P_n$.  Then $({\mathcal H}_n)$ is a sequence of mutually orthogonal closed
		subspaces of ${\mathcal H}$.  For each $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$, let ${\mathcal H}_S$ be the closed span of
		$\{{\mathcal H}_n:n\in S\}$, and $P_S$ the projection onto ${\mathcal H}_S$.  Then $\{P_S:S\subseteq\mathbb{N}\}$
		is a 1-discrete subset of ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal H})$ of cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$.  Since $2^{\aleph_0}>\aleph_0$,
		${\mathcal B}({\mathcal H})$ cannot be separable by \ref{epsilon-discrete}.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: If there is a proof that a statement $\varphi$ is provable in {ZF}{} (or any other recursively axiomatizable theory $T$), then there is an algorithm for finding a proof of $\varphi$ in {ZF}{} (or $T$).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since the axioms of the theory $T$ can be recursively  enumerated, and since a proof in $T$ is a finite sequence of sentences that satisfies strict and clear rules, one can enumerate all (formal) proofs in $T$. Knowing that $\varphi$ is provable in $T$, one knows that a proof for $\varphi$ will eventually appear in this list.
head: environment

label: Def.Sigma1n
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def.Sigma1n} Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma)$ be a standard Borel space. 
	A subset $\mathsf A$ of $\mathsf X$ is $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_1$ (or \emph{analytic})\footnote{This is equivalent to being an analytic 
		subset of $\mathsf X$ (i.e., a continuous image of a Borel subset of some Polish space) in some, or any, Polish topology on $\mathsf X$ (\cite[25.A]{Ke:Classical}, see also Theorem~\ref{T.Isomorphic} below).} if there are a standard Borel space ($\mathsf Y,\Sigma')$  and a Borel set $\mathsf B\subseteq \mathsf X\times \mathsf Y$ such that 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq.Sigma11}
	\mathsf A=\{x\in \mathsf X\mid (\exists y\in \mathsf Y) (x,y)\in \mathsf B\}.
	\end{equation}
	A subset $\mathsf A$ of $\mathsf X$ is $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_1$ (or \emph{coanalytic}) if there are a standard Borel space ($\mathsf Y,\Sigma')$  and a Borel set $\mathsf B\subseteq \mathsf X\times \mathsf Y$ such that 
	\[
	\mathsf A=\{x\in \mathsf X\mid (\forall y\in \mathsf Y) (x,y)\in \mathsf B\}.
	\]
	Equivalently, $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_1$ sets are complements of $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_1$ sets. 
	
	For $n\geq 1$, $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_{n+1}$ and $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_{n+1}$ sets are defined by recursion on $n$ as follows. A subset $\mathsf A$ of $\mathsf X$ is $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_{n+1}$ if there are a standard Borel space ($\mathsf Y,\Sigma')$  and a~$\boldsymbol\Pi^1_n$ set $\mathsf B\subseteq \mathsf X\times \mathsf Y$ such that 
	\[
	\mathsf A=\{x\in \mathsf X\mid (\exists y\in \mathsf Y) (x,y)\in \mathsf B\}.
	\] 
	A subset $\mathsf A$ of $\mathsf X$ is $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_{n+1}$ if there are a standard Borel space ($\mathsf Y,\Sigma')$  and a~$\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_n$ set $\mathsf B\subseteq \mathsf X\times \mathsf Y$ such that 
	\[
	\mathsf A=\{x\in \mathsf X\mid (\forall y\in \mathsf Y) (x,y)\in \mathsf B\}.
	\] 
	Equivalently, $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_n$ sets are complements of $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_n$ sets for all $n$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The following remark may be safely ignored by most readers, but there is a reason why we used boldface symbols $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ and $\boldsymbol\Pi$ in Definition~\ref{Def.Sigma1n}. The lightface notation $\Sigma^1_1$ is reserved for the class of sets $\mathsf A$ such that the Polish spaces $\mathsf X$ and $\mathsf Y$, as well as the Borel set $\mathsf B$, are effective (see \cite[40.B]{Ke:Classical}).  The technical details of the definition of `effective' are irrelevant for us, but there are only countably many recursive closed subsets of a given recursively presented Polish space. This for example includes the Cantor space,  $\mathbb R^n$ and ${\mathcal O}_n$ for all $n$ and all separable AF algebras whose $K_0$ group is presented by recursive relations, but not all separable AF algebras.  From here one proceeds to recursively define the lightface hierarchies $\Sigma^1_n$ and $\Pi^1_n$. Tools from effective descriptive set theory, and the structure of the poset of $\Sigma^1_1$ subsets of ${\mathcal P}(\mathbb{N})$ in particular, were famously used to prove the Glimm--Effros dichotomy (\cite{HaKeLo:GE}), but we will not need them here.

label: T.Isomorphic
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathsf X$ is a countable standard Borel space, then its Borel $\sigma$-algebra is equal to  ${\mathcal P}(\mathsf X)$, thus every two countable standard Borel spaces of the same cardinality are Borel-isomorphic. The second part is in this case vacuous.
	
	So it suffices to prove that every uncountable standard Borel space~$\mathsf X$ is Borel-isomorphic to the Cantor space~$K$. By Cantor--Bendixson analysis,~$\mathsf X$ contains a perfect subset (\cite[Theorem~6.4]{Ke:Classical}), hence there is a continuous injection from $K$ into $\mathsf X$. On the other hand, there is a Borel injection from $\mathsf X$ into $K$ (for an elegant proof of this fact due to Jenna Zomback see \cite[Lemma B.2.3]{farah2019combinatorial}). By the Borel version of the Schr\"oder--Bernstein theorem (\cite[Theorem~15.7]{Ke:Classical}), $\mathsf X$ is Borel-isomorphic to $K$.               
	
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
	                                                                                                                                                                      
	
	It remains to prove that a Borel isomorphism between Polish spaces preserves the projective hierarchy. 
	Clearly, a Borel isomorphism sends Borel sets to Borel sets.
	Suppose that $f\colon \mathsf X\to \mathsf Y$ is a Borel-measurable map between Polish spaces and that $\mathsf A\subseteq \mathsf X$ is a $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_1$ set. 
	Fix a standard Borel space~$\mathsf Z$ and  a Borel $\mathsf B\subseteq \mathsf X\times \mathsf Z$ such that $\mathsf A$ is the projection of $\mathsf B$. The graph of $f$ is a Borel subset of $\mathsf X\times \mathsf Y$. The following subset of $\mathsf X\times \mathsf Z\times \mathsf Y$: 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq.BorelIsomorphism}
		\{(b,a,f(a)): (b,a)\in \mathsf B\}
	\end{equation}
	is  an intersection of two Borel sets and therefore Borel, and its  projection to $\mathsf Y$ is equal to $f[\mathsf A]$. 
	This implies that~$\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_1$ sets are preserved by Borel-isomorphisms, and the statement for~$\boldsymbol\Pi^1_1$ sets follows by taking complements. 
	
	Suppose that  $n$ is such that every Borel isomorphism between standard Borel spaces sends $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_n$ sets to $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_n$ sets and $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_n$ sets to $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_n$ sets. Fix a Borel isomorphism between standard Borel spaces $f\colon \mathsf X\to \mathsf Y$. The proof that the image of a $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_n$ set $\mathsf A\subseteq \mathsf X$ under a Borel map $f$ is $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_{n+1}$ is analogous to the proof in case when $n=0$: Fix a $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_{n}$ set $\mathbf B\subseteq \mathsf X\times \mathsf Z$, note that the set in \eqref{eq.BorelIsomorphism} is an intersection of a $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_n$ set and a Borel set, and therefore $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_n$. Its projection to $\mathsf Y$ is equal to $f[\mathsf A]$. 
	By taking complements, this conclusion extends to~$\boldsymbol\Pi^1_{n+1}$ sets and completes the proof of the inductive step.

title: Lemma
body_md:
Suppose that $(\mathsf X_j,\Sigma_j)$, for $j<n+1$,  are standard Borel spaces and that $\mathsf Y\subseteq \prod_{j<n+1} \mathsf X_j$ belongs to the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the rectangles with sides in $\Sigma_j$. 
	
	Then every formula of the form 
	\[
	(\exists^1 x_1)(\forall^1 x_2) (\exists^1 x_3)\dots (Q x_n) \varphi(\bar x, y)\in \mathsf Y
	\]
	where $Q$ is $\exists^1$ if $n$ is odd and $\forall^1$ if $n$ is even, is $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_n$ and every formula of the form 
		\[
	(\forall^1 x_1)(\exists^1 x_2) (\forall^1 x_3)\dots (Q x_n) (\bar x, y)\in \mathsf Y, 
	\]
	where $Q$ is $\forall^1$ if $n$ is odd and $\exists^1$ if $n$ is even, is $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_n$. \qed

title: Definition
body_md:
A subset $\mathsf A$ of a standard Borel space defined by a formula in parameters $\bar a$ is \emph{absolute for transitive models of ZF} if for every transitive model $M$ of {ZF}{} such that $\bar a$ belongs to $M$ we have $\mathsf A^M=\mathsf A\cap M$. 
	
	A formula $\varphi$ (possibly with parameters $\bar a$) is \emph{absolute for transitive models of ZF} if for every transitive model $M$ of {ZF}{} such that the parameters of $\varphi$ belong to~$M$,  $\varphi^M$ is equivalent to $\varphi$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
If $\mathsf X$ is a set, then a tree on $\mathsf X$ is a set $\mathsf T\subseteq \bigcup_n \mathsf X^n$ which is hereditary, in the sense that $t\in \mathsf T$ implies  all of its initial segments belong to $\mathsf T$. 
 For $s$ and $t$ we write $s\sqsubset t$ if $s$ is a proper initial segment of $t$. 
A \emph{branch} of $\mathsf T$ is $x\in \mathsf X^\mathbb{N}$ such that $x\restriction m\in \mathsf T$ for all $m\in \mathbb{N}$. 
It is convenient to turn trees upside down, and a tree is called \emph{well-founded} if it has no infinite branches.
head: environment

label: L.TreeRank
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{L.TreeRank} If $M$ is a transitive model of {ZF}{} and $\mathsf T\in M$ is a tree on some  set $\mathsf X$, then the assertion `$\mathsf T$ is well-founded' is absolute between $M$ and any transitive model $N$ of {ZF}{} (including the universe itself) that includes~$M$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $M$ is transitive, we have $\mathsf X\subseteq M$. If $\mathsf T$ has an infinite branch $x$ in $M$, then $x$ is still an infinite branch in $N$. Assume $\mathsf T$ is well-founded in~$M$.  Recursively define
	rank function $\rho_\mathsf T$ from $\mathsf T$ into the ordinals by 
	\[
	\rho_\mathsf T(s)=\sup\{\rho_\mathsf T(t): s\sqsubset t, t\in \mathsf T\}+1. 
	\]
	The supremum of the range of $\rho_\mathsf T$ is an ordinal of cardinality no greater than that of~$\mathsf T$, and since $M$ is a model of {ZF}{} this ordinal is included in $M$. 
	
	Since $\mathsf T$ is well-founded, the domain of $\rho_\mathsf T$ is equal to $\mathsf T$ and $s\sqsubset t$ implies $\rho_\mathsf T(s)>\rho_\mathsf T(t)$.  If $x$ is an infinite branch of $\mathsf T$ in $N$, then $\rho_\mathsf T(x\restriction n)$, for $n\in \mathbb{N}$, is an infinite decreasing sequence of ordinals; contradiction.
head: environment

label: T.Analytic
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq.A=p[T]
title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove the statement for $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_1$ sets. By transitivity (of logical equivalence, pun not intended), it also suffices to prove absoluteness between a fixed transitive model of ${ZF}$ and the universe.  We first prove  absoluteness for $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_1$ subsets of the Baire space ${\mathbb{N}}^{\mathbb{N}}$. For every analytic subset $\mathsf A$ of ${\mathbb{N}}^{\mathbb{N}}$ there is a closed $\mathsf B\subseteq ({\mathbb{N}}^{\mathbb{N}})^2$ such that $\mathsf A$ is the projection of $\mathsf B$. Let 
	\[
	\mathsf T=\{(x\restriction n,y\restriction n): (x,y)\in \mathsf B, n\in \mathbb{N}\}. 
	\]
	Then $\mathsf T$ is a tree on $\mathbb{N}\times \mathbb{N}$ and 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq.A=p[T]}
	\mathsf A=\{x\in {\mathbb{N}}^{\mathbb{N}}: (\exists y\in {\mathbb{N}}^{\mathbb{N}}) (x\restriction n,y\restriction n)\in \mathsf T\}. 
	\end{equation}
In other words, writing (by $|s|$ we denote the length of $s$)
\[
\mathsf T_x=\{s: (x\restriction |s|,s)\in \mathsf T\}
\]
we have that $\mathsf A$ is the set of all $x$ such that $\mathsf T_x$ is ill-founded. By Lemma~\ref{L.TreeRank}, the latter assertion is absolute for transitive models of {ZF}{} and therefore for $x\in M$ we have that $x\in \mathsf A^M$ if and only if $x\in \mathsf A$, as required. 

For subsets of an arbitrary Polish space $\mathsf X$,  Theorem~\ref{T.Isomorphic} implies that~$\mathsf X$ is Borel-isomorphic to ${\mathbb{N}}^{\mathbb{N}}$ and that  the isomorphism is definable from an enumeration of a countable generating subset of $\Sigma$, and absolute for transitive models of ZF. Since Borel-isomorphism sends $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_n$ sets to $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_n$ sets, the conclusion follows.

label: T.Shoenfield
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T.Shoenfield}
	Every $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$ set, and every $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$ statement,  is absolute for transitive models of {ZF}{} that contain the parameter from which the set is defined and all countable ordinals.
head: environment

title: Guide to the Proof of Theorem \refT.Shoenfield
body_md:
As in the proof of Theorem~\ref{T.Analytic}, it suffices to prove the statement for $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$ subsets of ${\mathbb{N}}^{\mathbb{N}}$.  The proof in this case  can be found in the literature (\cite[Corollary~7.15]{drake1974set}, \cite[Theorem~8F.10]{Mo:Descriptive}, \cite[Theorem~13.15]{kanamori2008higher};  in \cite[\S 36.D]{Ke:Classical} the key object for the proof, a Shoenfield tree, is defined for other purposes).  
	The salient point is that the Shoenfield tree is a tree $\mathsf T$ on $\mathbb{N}\times \aleph_1$ such that $\mathsf A$ satisfies the analog of equation~\eqref{eq.A=p[T]}, $x\in \mathsf A$ if and only if $\mathsf T_x$ has an infinite branch, and Lemma~\ref{L.TreeRank} applies .

label: C.IllFounded
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{C.IllFounded}
	Every $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$ or $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_2$ statement $\varphi$ is absolute between any two models $M_1$ and $M_2$ of {ZF}{} which are transitive and contain all countable ordinals (and parameters of $\varphi$) in the interpretation of "transitive" and "all countable ordinals" within some model $M$ of {ZF}{} that has both $M_1$ and $M_2$ as elements, or as definable classes.  \qed

title: Corollary

Every $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$ or $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_2$ statement  $\varphi$  with parameters $x$ is absolute between  $M$ and $L[x]^M$ for any model $M$ of {ZF}.

label: T.Provability
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T.Provability}
Every $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$ statement, and every   $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_2$ statement,  that is provable in {ZFC}{} or even in {ZF}\, +\, $V=L$  (or $V=L[x]$, if $\varphi$ has a parameter  coded by $x$) is provable in {ZF}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\varphi$ that is $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$ or $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_2$ and provable in {ZF}\,+\,$V=L[x]$, where $x\in {\mathcal P}(\mathbb{N})$ codes the parameters of $\varphi$. 
		Fix a model $M$ of {ZF}{} that contains $x$. This code can be chosen in any recursively defined Polish space, and  it will be convenient to choose $x$ in ${\mathcal P}(\mathbb{N})$. By our assumption, $\varphi$ holds is $L[x]^M$ (i.e., $L[x]$ as computed in $M$) and by  Corollary~\ref{C.IllFounded-with-parameters}, $\varphi$ is absolute between  $M$ and $L[X]^M$. 	
	Since $M$ was an arbitrary model that contains $x$, this proves that $\varphi$ holds in every model of {ZF}{} that contains $x$. 
By the Completeness Theorem of first-order logic, it follows that $\varphi$ is a theorem of {ZF}.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Assume $\varphi$ is a  $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$ statement or a $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_2$ statement  and that in addition it satisfies one of the following. 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\varphi$ follows from {ZFC}+{OCA$_T$}+{MA}. 
		\item $\varphi$ follows from {ZFC}+$\diamondsuit_{\aleph_1}$. 
		\item \label{T.Provable.3} $\varphi$ holds in some forcing extension of the constructible universe $L$.
	\end{enumerate} 
	Then $\varphi$ is provable in {ZF}. 
	\qed
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a unital separable $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A$ and $x\in A$. 
	We need to prove that there is a state $\varphi$ on $A$ such that $\varphi(x^*x)=\|x\|^2$. This is a result of {ZFC}, and in order to conclude that it can be proved in ZF, by Theorem~\ref{T.Shoenfield} it will suffice to prove that this is a $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_2$ statement with code for $A$ as a parameter. 
	
	
	
	Since the map $(a,\varphi)\mapsto \varphi(a)$ is jointly continuous on $A\times \mathsf S(A)$, the set 
	\[
	Z=\{(a,\varphi)\in A\times \mathsf S(A)\mid \varphi(a^*a)=\|a\|^2\}
	\]
	is a closed subset of $A\times \mathsf S(A)$, which is a product of two Polish spaces ($A$ is Polish by the assumption and $\mathsf S(A)$ is Polish by Lemma~\ref{L.S(A)}).
	
	Therefore the statement $(\forall a\in A)(\exists \varphi\in \mathsf S(A))\varphi(a^*a)=\|a\|^2$ is $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_2$. Thus this is a  theorem of {ZF}{} by Theorem~\ref{T.Shoenfield}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $n\geq 1$ and  commuting normal elements $a_1,\dots, a_n$  of a $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A$.  We first need to prove that $\operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)$ is nonempty.
	
Since the standard proof that the joint spectrum of  an $n$-tuple of normal operators does not change when passing to a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-subalgebra does not require any Choice,   
	by replacing $A$ with $\mathrm{C}^*(\bar a,1)$ we may assume that it is separable. Fix a countable dense subset $D$ of $A$. Let 
	\[
\textstyle	B=\{(\bar \lambda, \bar b)\in \mathbb{C}^n\times D^n\mid \|\sum_{j\leq n} b_j (a_j-\lambda_j 1)-1\|<1 \}. 
	\]
We claim that $\bar \lambda\in \operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)$ if and only if $(\forall \bar b\in D^n)(\bar \lambda, \bar b)\notin B$. Suppose that $\bar \lambda\in \operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)$ and fix $b\in D^n$. Since $a_j-\lambda_j 1$, for $j\leq n$,  generate  a proper ideal, $x=\sum_{j\leq n} b_j (a_j-\lambda_j 1)$ is not invertible, and in particular $\|x-1\|\geq 1$. Therefore $(\bar \lambda, \bar b)\notin B$. 
Conversely, suppose that $\bar \lambda\notin \operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)$. Then the ideal generated by $a_j-\lambda_j 1$, for $j\leq n$, is improper and $\sum_j d_j (a_j-\lambda_j 1)=1$. Since~$D$ is dense, we can find $\bar b$ such that $(\bar \lambda ,\bar b)\in B$. 


 Since $\bar b$ ranges over the countable set $D^n$, and since the section of $B$ at each $\bar b$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{C}^n$, we conclude that $\mathbb{C}^n\setminus \operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{C}^n$. Therefore $\operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)$ is closed, and the assertion that it is nonempty is~$\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_1$, and therefore absolute by Theorem~\ref{T.Shoenfield}. Since  it is a theorem of {ZFC}{} (\cite{Arv:Short}), the conclusion follows. 
Since the joint spectrum of $\bar a$ is included in the bounded set $\{\bar \lambda : |\lambda_j|\leq \|a_j\|$ for all $j\leq n\}$, it is a closed and bounded  subset of $\mathbb{C}^n$ and therefore compact. 

It remains to prove that if $f$ is a complex *-polynomial in $2n$ variables, then 
\begin{multline*}
\sigma(f(a_1,\dots, a_n, a_1^*,\dots, a_n^*))\\
=\{f(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, \bar\lambda_1, \dots, \bar\lambda_n)\mid (\lambda_1,\dots, \lambda_n)\in \operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)\}. 
\end{multline*}
Fix such $f$. Then the sets 
	$X=\sigma(f(a_1,\dots, a_n, a_1^*,\dots, a_n^*))$ and $\operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)$ are compact by the first part of this Theorem. The continuous image of the latter, $Y=\{f(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, \bar\lambda_1, \dots, \bar\lambda_n)\mid (\lambda_1,\dots, \lambda_n)\in \operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a)\}$ is therefore also compact. 

	Finally, the assertion that $X=Y$ is $\boldsymbol\Pi^1_1$ because it asserts that the symmetric difference of $X$ and $Y$ (a Borel set) is empty, i.e., that $(\forall \lambda\in \mathbb{C})(\lambda\notin X\Delta Y)$. Therefore, Theorem~\ref{T.Shoenfield} implies that these two sets are equal.

label: FullFunctCalc
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{FullFunctCalc}
	Let $A$ be a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra, $n\geq 1$, and let $\bar a$ be an $n$-tuple of commuting normal operators.  Then $p\mapsto p(\bar a)$ ($p$ is a complex *-polynomial in $n$ commuting variables)
	extends to an isometric
	isomorphism from $C(\operatorname{j\sigma}(\bar a))$ onto the uniformly closed subalgebra of $A$
	generated by $\bar a$ and~1.  If $\bar a$ is closed under adjoints, this is $\mathrm{C}^*(\bar a,1)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix disjoint convex subsets $A$ and $B$ of a separable normed space~$X$ such that $A$ is open. By replacing $B$ with its closure, we may assume   $B$ is closed. As open and closed subsets of a Polish space $X$, both $A$ and $B$ are coded by real parameters. 


In the following we write $X_m$, $X^*_m$ for the $m$-balls in $X$ and $X^*$. 
While $X^*_m$ is not necessarily norm-separable, it is compact and metrizable in the weak$^*$-topology, and we will consider it with the corresponding Borel structure. 

The duality map  from $X\times X^*$ into the scalars, $(\xi,\varphi)\mapsto \varphi(\xi)$,  is jointly continuous on  $X_m\times X^*_n$, when $X$ is considered with the norm topology and~$X^*$ with the weak*-topology,  for all $m,n\geq 1$. This is because for all $\xi,\eta$ in $X_m$ and all $\varphi,\psi$ in $X^*_n$ we have that 
\[
|\psi(\eta)-\varphi(\xi)|
\leq |\psi(\eta-\xi)|+|(\psi-\varphi)(\xi)|
\leq n\|\eta-\xi\|+|(\psi-\varphi)(\xi)|.
\]
The first term is uniformly small when $\eta$ is norm-close to $\xi$, and the second is controlled by a basic weak-* neighbourhood evaluated at $\xi$.
The set 
\begin{align*}
Z=\{(\varphi, \xi, \eta,r): \varphi\in X^*, \ &\xi\notin A\text{ or }\xi\in A\text{  and }\Re(\varphi(\xi))<r, \text{ and }   \\
&\eta\notin B \text{ or  }\eta\in B\text{ and }r\leq \Re(\varphi(\eta)))\}
\end{align*}
is therefore a Borel subset of $X^*\times X^2\times \mathbb R$, and the existence of a linear functional that separates $A$ from $B$ is equivalent to 
\[
(\exists\varphi)(\exists r)(\forall \xi,\eta\in X)(\varphi,\xi,\eta,r)\in Z. 
\]
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                         
                                                                      
This is a $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$ statement (with codes for $X$, $A$, and $B$ as parameters), hence it is absolute between transitive models of {ZF}{} that contain all countable ordinals. Since it is a theorem of {ZFC}, it is a theorem of {ZF}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $K$ is a compact convex subset of the dual of a separable Banach space $X$. 
By the Banach--Alaoglu theorem, $K$ is a compact metrizable space.  Fix a compatible metric $d$ on $K$. 
The extreme boundary of $K$ is equal to 
\[
\partial K=\bigcap_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\{x\in K\mid (\forall y,z\in K)x=(y+z)/2\text{ implies } d(y,z)<1/n\}.
\]
Since the set $\{(y+z)/2: y,z\in K, d(y,z)\geq 1/n\}$ is compact (as a continuous image of a compact set), the set $\partial K$ is a $G_\delta$ set. The assertion that this~$G_\delta$ set is nonempty is $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_1$ (it involves a code for $K$ as a parameter, thus the boldface), and therefore absolute between transitive models of {ZF}{} by the $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_1$ Absoluteness Theorem (Theorem~\ref{T.Analytic}). Since it is a theorem of {ZFC}{} that every compact convex set has an extremal point, this is also a theorem of {ZF}{} by Theorem~\ref{T.Provability}.  

                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
In order to prove that every  separable compact convex set in a locally convex space is the closed convex hull of its extreme points, assume otherwise. Consider the closed convex hull  $C$ of $\partial K$ and fix $x\in K\setminus C$. By the Hahn--Banach separation theorem (Proposition~\ref{P.HBetc} \eqref{5.BS.HBs}) there are  a continuous affine function $\phi\colon K\to \mathbb R$ and $r\in \mathbb R$ such that $\phi(x)\leq r<\phi(y)$ for all $y\in C$. Then $K$ has a face exposed by $\phi$ that is disjoint from $C$. By the first part of the proof, this face has an extremal point, and such point is an extremal point of $K$;  contradiction.

label: P.not-axiomatizable
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P.not-axiomatizable}
	While it is provable in {ZFC}{} that having a tracial state is axiomatizable, this is not provable in  {ZF}+{DC}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The property of having a tracial state is  axiomatizable in continuous logic by  \cite[Theorem~2.5.1]{Muenster}. This proof uses an abstract characterization of axiomatizability via ultraproducts. 


We will prove that in some model of {ZF}{} there are elementarily equivalent $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebras $A$ and $B$ such that $B$ has a tracial state and $A$ does not. Once proved, this will imply that having a tracial state is not axiomatizable. 
As pointed out in \ref{P.ExistenceOfStates}, (see also \ref{P.ExistenceOfStates.1}) the commutative $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A=\ell^\infty(\mathbb{N})/c_0(\mathbb{N})$ has no states (tracial or otherwise) if all sets of reals have the Property of Baire. A model with this property in which {DC}{} holds was constructed starting from a model of {ZFC}{} in \cite[Corollary~7.17]{shelah1984can}. 
 Since {DC}{} implies \AC$_\omega$, in this model $\operatorname{Sep}(A) $ is $\sigma$-complete and therefore the downwards L\"owenheim--Skolem Theorem\footnote{We would like to thank Asaf Karagila for pointing out that {DC}{} is equivalent to the downwards  L\"owenheim--Skolem theorem (Boolos, see \cite[Theorem~3.4]{aspero2021dependent}).}  (\cite[Theorem~7.1.9]{farah2019combinatorial}) implies that $A$ is elementarily equivalent to some of its separable $\mathrm{C}^*$-subalgebras. Every commutative, separable $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra~$B$ is isomorphic to $C(X)$ for a compact metrizable space $X$ (Lemma~\ref{L.S(A)}) and in particular has tracial states.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: The statement `Every unital stably finite $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra has a tracial state' is absolute between transitive models of {ZFC}{} that contain all countable ordinals.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove (using AC) that if there is  a stably finite $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra without a tracial state then there is one that is in addition separable. 
If $A$ is a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra, and every separable unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-subalgebra $B$ has a tracial state
$\tau_B$, extend $\tau_B$ to a state $\phi_B$ on $A$; then any cluster point of the net $(\phi_B)$
is a tracial state on $A$. Since being tracial is a closed condition, this cluster point is a tracial state.
